# 18-Month Direct Export Transition Plan
## Oaxaca Coffee Cooperative (40 members, ~60 ha total)

## Reality Check First

Direct export requires paying for: harvest labor, processing, storage, certification audits, export documentation, container freight, and financing the 60-90+ day gap between shipment and payment from a foreign buyer. A cooperative with zero working capital between harvests **cannot self-finance this transition**. Any plan pretending otherwise will collapse at the first cash crunch. So this plan is explicit about the split.

---

## What Requires External Finance (No Way Around It)

1. **Export working capital loan** — the single largest need. Even with a signed contract, someone must pay members for cherry/parchment at harvest, months before the importer pays. Estimate: $40,000–$70,000 USD depending on volume (roughly $1,000–1,800/member if paying comparable-to-intermediary prices).
2. **Certification costs** — Organic and/or Fair Trade certification audits run $1,500–$4,000/year for a group this size, plus 1-3 years of "in-conversion" period with no price premium if not already certified.
3. **Wet mill / dry mill upgrades** — if cherry is currently sold to the intermediary partially processed, the co-op likely lacks adequate depulping, fermentation, drying (patios/parabolic dryers), and storage infrastructure to meet export moisture/defect specs. $15,000–$40,000.
4. **Quality control equipment** — moisture meters, sample roaster, cupping setup: $3,000–$6,000.
5. **Legal/export registration costs** — forming or upgrading legal entity, export permits, phytosanitary certificates, SENASICA registration, tax ID for export: $2,000–$5,000.
6. **First container logistics** — trucking to port, customs broker, freight forwarder, ocean freight: $3,000–$6,000 per container, usually payable before or at shipment.

**Likely sources**: Mexican development finance (FIRA, Financiera Nacional), NGO/impact lenders (Root Capital, Rabobank Foundation, Oikocredit), buyer pre-financing (many specialty roasters advance 20-30% on signed contracts), or state (Oaxaca) agricultural programs. Root Capital specifically specializes in exactly this bridge loan for coffee co-ops and should be a first call.

---

## What the Co-op CAN Do Without Any External Money

- Organize legally / formalize governance
- Build member consensus and by-laws for the new model
- Inventory and grade existing infrastructure honestly
- Start record-keeping for traceability (a prerequisite for certification, free to start)
- Cup and profile their own coffee (if any member or nearby university/INMECAFE-successor agency will donate cupping time)
- Contact buyers, attend/apply to virtual events, build relationships
- Apply for grants and loans (writing applications costs time, not capital)
- Negotiate a *transitional* deal with the current intermediary or a new one for partial volume while learning export mechanics

---

## Month-by-Month Plan

### Months 1–3: Foundation (near-zero cost)
- Form or confirm a legal entity capable of exporting (e.g., formalize as a Sociedad Cooperativa or similar with export capacity — many co-ops already have this but haven't activated export registration)
- Elect/confirm an export committee (3-5 members) distinct from day-to-day co-op leadership
- Conduct honest infrastructure audit: current wet/dry processing capacity, storage, cupping ability
- Begin traceability record-keeping per member plot (yield, harvest dates, lot separation)
- Research and shortlist 3-5 financing sources (Root Capital, FIRA, Rabobank Foundation, Oaxaca state programs)
- Draft grant/loan applications — this is the critical path item; delays here delay everything

### Months 4–6: Finance & Certification Push
- Submit loan/grant applications (expect 2-4 month decision cycles — start early, this is why it's Month 4 not Month 10)
- If pursuing organic certification: enroll with certifier now, since transition period (1-3 years) starts from enrollment, not from harvest
- Continue negotiating with current intermediary for interim sales — **do not cut this cord yet**; it remains the co-op's cash lifeline until export income is proven
- Begin outreach to 10-15 potential specialty buyers (importers, roasters) with samples from best available lots, even if only in small non-export quantities, to gauge interest and get quality feedback
- Get informal price/cupping feedback — this costs nothing but travel and shipping small samples

### Months 7–9: Decision Point
- **If financing is secured**: proceed to infrastructure investment (dry mill upgrades, storage, QC equipment) timed to be ready before the next harvest (typically Nov-Feb depending on the region)
- **If financing is NOT secured**: this is the honest fork. The co-op should not attempt full direct export this cycle. Fallback: negotiate an improved-terms contract with an ethical importer who will pay a partial premium without full independence yet, or pursue direct export for a small pilot volume (5-10%) using only members' pooled contributions, while continuing traditional sales for the bulk
- Sign at minimum a Letter of Intent or forward contract with 1-2 buyers — this LOI is often required as collateral for the working capital loan, so buyer outreach and financing applications happen in parallel, not sequentially

### Months 10–12: Harvest Execution
- Disburse working capital loan to pay members at harvest (this is the concrete moment external finance becomes non-optional — without it members go unpaid and revert to the intermediary out of necessity)
- Execute quality-controlled processing per lot, following traceability protocol established in Months 1-3
- Cup and grade all lots; separate export-quality from lower grades (lower grades still sell locally/regionally — don't force everything into export that isn't ready)
- Finalize export-quality volume against buyer commitments

### Months 13–15: First Export Shipment
- Complete export documentation (phytosanitary cert, certificate of origin, commercial invoice, packing list)
- Contract customs broker and freight forwarder
- Ship first container(s) — likely 1-2 containers (18-36 tons) given the co-op's size, not the full harvest
- **Critical**: do not commit 100% of harvest to export in year one. Reserve capacity to sell remainder through existing channels in case of quality rejection, shipping delay, or buyer payment delay

### Months 16–18: Repayment, Evaluation, Second Cycle Prep
- Receive buyer payment (typically 30-60-90 days post-shipment/bill of lading — plan cash flow assuming 90)
- Repay working capital loan from proceeds
- Distribute member payments — compare honestly against what the intermediary would have paid; this comparison is the real test of whether the transition was worth it
- Conduct full financial and quality post-mortem with all members
- Reapply for larger working capital facility for Year 2 based on demonstrated repayment history — this is when financing terms should improve significantly

---

## What Success Looks Like at Month 18

Not full independence — a **partial, proven pipeline**: 20-40% of volume moving direct export with a track record that unlocks larger, cheaper financing for Year 2, while the intermediary or secondary buyers still absorb the rest. Co-ops that try to flip 100% of volume to direct export in one cycle without financing history very commonly fail, default, or get quality/logistics disasters that push them back to intermediaries permanently. The realistic win is a functioning minority channel with clean books and buyer trust — not full displacement in 18 months.
